query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled level of carbon doping into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will enhance their glass‐forming ability and improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to similar alloys without carbon.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) produced under conventional conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a specific, controlled amount of carbon into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The intervention is effective when the alloy is processed under rapid solidification conditions (e.g., melt-spinning) that are marginal for amorphization; the predicted benefits will be reduced if carbon concentration falls outside an optimal window or if cooling rates are either too high or too low.
generation.structural_mediator: Carbon atoms intercalate within the alloy matrix, disrupting crystalline nucleation sites and increasing local disorder, possibly by forming localized bonds with phosphorus and transition metals.
generation.mechanism: By increasing local atomic disorder and effectively elevating the configurational entropy, carbon doping retards the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling, thereby lowering the critical cooling rate needed for glass formation and raising the temperature at which the amorphous phase crystallizes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloy will exhibit a lower critical cooling rate for amorphization and a higher crystallization onset temperature (as measured by DSC) than its undoped counterpart.
generation.baseline: An otherwise comparable phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy synthesized and processed under identical conditions but without carbon doping.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within an optimal carbon concentration range and under rapid solidification conditions; outside these conditions (e.g., with excessive or insufficient carbon, or under extreme cooling rates), the improvement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal carbon concentration and the magnitude of the improvements in thermal stability and glass-forming ability remain to be determined quantitatively.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples based on a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20): one with a controlled carbon doping (e.g., 1-3 at.%) and one without. Process both sets using rapid quenching (melt-spinning) to induce amorphization. Characterize the samples using DSC to determine crystallization onset temperatures, X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, and electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructural analysis.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure crystallization onset temperature
XRD to verify amorphous versus crystalline structures
Determination of the critical cooling rate for achieving an amorphous state
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature and a reduced critical cooling rate compared to the undoped samples, or if carbon addition leads to the formation of unintended crystalline or deleterious secondary phases, the hypothesis should be rejected.

Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components.
